---
title: "2 · Random Matrix Theory"
---

A chaotic quantum system has no obvious small parameter, yet its **spectrum** is
remarkably universal: the fine-grained statistics of its energy levels match
those of a *random matrix* with the same symmetries. This is the Bohigas–
Giannoni–Schmit observation, and it is the first concrete sense in which "quantum
chaos" can be measured.

The key phenomenon is **level repulsion** — eigenvalues of a random matrix avoid
each other, unlike the independent levels of an integrable system. How strongly
they repel depends only on a time-reversal symmetry, giving the three
Wigner–Dyson classes (orthogonal, unitary, symplectic). This part derives the
repulsion directly from the eigenvalue measure and checks the universal spacing
and moment statistics numerically.

What you'll take away: the **Wigner surmise**, the **semicircle law** and its
combinatorics, and the gap-ratio statistic you'll reuse in Chapter 4 to detect
chaos without unfolding a spectrum.

## Notebooks in this part

- [Level repulsion in the GOE](../notebooks/ch2/solution_ch2_goe_spacing.ipynb) — deriving the Wigner surmise for nearest-neighbour spacings.
- [Moments of the Wigner semicircle](../notebooks/ch2/solution_ch2_semicircle_moments.ipynb) — the Catalan-number combinatorics behind the density.
- [Eigenphase repulsion in the CUE](../notebooks/ch2/solution_ch2_cue_eigenphase.ipynb) — the same physics for unitaries on the circle.
